She remembered a moment a few summers ago when her family was in Vermont after attending a classical performance of Mozart.

They were “just sitting around and having a glass of wine, and laughing and talking about family and life and what was going on in our lives,” she said. The Harrises “could never get enough information about what all their nieces and nephews and family members were doing.”

“It’s really the last time I can remember us all sitting around as a family, and I’m so glad that I have that memory,” she said.

Ten were employees of French electrical equipment supplier CGED, according to Agence France-Presse. Nine of those employees had won the trip to Rio from CGED because of their strong work performance, AFP reported.

“There was a competition for the best sales reps ... and nine of them won and went to Brazil for four days,” CGED Chief Executive Laurent Bouveresse told AFP.

“They were my two best friends. I just hope she knows I loved her.”

“They loved life, loved everyone,” Charlstie Laytin said during a telephone interview Wednesday. She said the family hoped the couple would be remembered for how they lived rather than for the tragedy that ended their lives. “We’re all just devastated and going to miss them both so much,” she added.

The Harrises were among three Americans aboard Air France Flight 447, which crashed Monday. The aircraft was traveling from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, to Paris, France, with 228 passengers and crew members when it went down about four hours after departure. Investigators had not yet established what caused the crash, and no official list identifying the victims was available as of Wednesday afternoon.

Anne Harris’ sister, Mary Miley, said the couple lived in Rio de Janeiro. Michael Harris, 60, worked there as a geologist for Devon Energy, an independent U.S.-based oil and natural gas producer, according to a company spokesman. Miley said the couple was headed to Paris for both a training seminar and a vacation.

Laytin described her aunt and uncle as optimistic people who always viewed life positively. She called her uncle a “ham” who could make others laugh even on difficult days.

She recalled a family gathering in Vermont several summers earlier, after they had attended a classical performance of Mozart. The relatives spent the evening drinking wine, laughing and discussing their family, their lives and recent events. Laytin said Anne and Michael were endlessly interested in hearing what their nieces, nephews and other family members were doing.

That gathering, she said, was the most recent occasion she could remember when the entire family had simply sat together, and she was grateful to still have the memory.

Laytin said her relatives hoped investigators would soon learn what happened to the plane. She explained that the first shock was beginning to fade as the reality of the couple’s deaths took hold. The family’s grieving process had started, she said, and everyone was concentrating on supporting one another and beginning to heal.

Most of those aboard Flight 447 were from Brazil, France and Germany. The other victims represented 29 additional countries.

Agence France-Presse reported that 10 people on the flight worked for CGED, a French supplier of electrical equipment. Nine had earned the trip to Rio as a reward for strong job performance. CGED chief executive Laurent Bouveresse told AFP that the company had held a contest for its top sales representatives, with nine winners receiving a four-day trip to Brazil. Each winner could bring a friend or partner, and a company executive also joined the group, he said. CNN made several unsuccessful attempts to contact CGED representatives.

Another pair believed to have been aboard the plane was engaged couple Julia Schmidt, from Brazil, and Alex Crolow, from Germany. Their friend Brian Buzby, of Houston, Texas, spoke about them to CNN affiliate KTRK.

Buzby said he met Schmidt and Crolow when all three attended Bucerius Law School in Germany. KTRK reported that they completed their studies the previous August.

According to Buzby, Crolow was taking Schmidt home so they could tell her mother they planned to marry. He said he hoped they had not suffered and found some comfort in believing they were together, because he would not have wanted either of them to face the ordeal alone.

Calling them his two best friends, Buzby added that he hoped Schmidt knew he loved her.

The Airbus A330 crashed in the equatorial Atlantic after encountering problems at cruising altitude. The wreckage was not located on the ocean floor until nearly two years later, prolonging uncertainty for families. Investigators ultimately concluded that temporary loss of reliable airspeed information and the crew’s subsequent actions led to an aerodynamic stall.

# Beyond the Passenger List: How the Victims of Air France Flight 447 Were Remembered

**RIO DE JANEIRO —** Air France Flight 447 carried 228 people when it left Rio de Janeiro for Paris on the night of May 31, 2009. They came from more than 30 countries and included children, business travelers, musicians, doctors, researchers, tourists and 12 crew members.

In the first days after the aircraft disappeared over the Atlantic, their identities were often reduced to numbers: 216 passengers, 12 crew members, 61 French citizens, 58 Brazilians and 26 Germans, along with people from countries across Europe, the Americas, Africa and Asia.

But their families and friends resisted that accounting. In memorial services, newspaper tributes, professional gatherings and private recollections, they spoke instead about the lives behind the manifest — about talent, friendship, public service, humor, curiosity and plans that had not yet been fulfilled.

For those left behind, Flight 447 was not primarily a story about an aircraft. It was the story of people who had been going home, returning to work, beginning holidays or continuing lives that seemed ordinary until they were abruptly lost.

## Three young doctors remembered in Ireland

Among the passengers were three Irish doctors — **Aisling Butler, Jane Deasy and Eithne Walls** — who were returning from a holiday in Brazil.

Their deaths were felt especially deeply in Ireland’s medical community, where colleagues remembered them not simply as promising physicians but as compassionate young women who had chosen careers devoted to other people.

Walls had also performed with *Riverdance* before studying medicine. Tributes recalled the discipline and energy with which she pursued both dancing and medical work. Friends described her as someone whose achievements never displaced her warmth or loyalty.

Butler and Deasy were similarly remembered for their intelligence, generosity and dedication to patients. Hospitals, schools and local communities mourned them together, while their families emphasized the distinct personality and promise of each woman.

The three friends became among the most widely recognized victims in Ireland. Yet those closest to them repeatedly sought to keep attention on how they had lived: as daughters, sisters, friends and doctors at the beginning of careers that had already touched many lives.

## Musicians whose work continued to be heard

The flight also carried internationally respected musicians.

**Silvio Barbato**, a Brazilian conductor and composer, had worked with major orchestras and opera companies and was known for promoting Brazilian music. He had conducted at prominent venues, including Rio de Janeiro’s Municipal Theatre, and had built a career that linked Brazil’s musical traditions with the wider classical world.

After his death, fellow musicians remembered his enthusiasm, intellectual energy and belief in music as a public art. Performances and tributes kept his compositions and interpretations before audiences, allowing his work to remain part of Brazil’s cultural life.

**Fatma Ceren Necipoğlu**, a Turkish harpist and academic, was also aboard. She taught at Anadolu University and had performed internationally. Students and colleagues remembered her not only for her technical skill but also for the care she gave to young musicians.

Her name later became associated with concerts and harp events in Turkey. For her family, students and fellow performers, music provided a way to preserve her presence: each performance offered a reminder that her influence had not ended with the flight.

## Researchers devoted to reducing violence

**Pablo Dreyfus**, an Argentine researcher, and his wife, **Ana Carolina Rodrigues**, a Brazilian specialist in human rights and public security, were returning to Europe together.

Both had devoted their professional lives to understanding and reducing armed violence. Dreyfus was known for research on illicit firearms, weapons trafficking and public security in Latin America. Rodrigues worked on related issues, including the human consequences of violence and insecurity.

Their colleagues remembered them as more than policy experts. They were described as principled, energetic people who believed research should serve communities and save lives. Their deaths were a personal loss to friends and relatives and a professional loss to a network of activists and scholars working on arms control and violence prevention.

Those who honored them stressed the meaning of the work they had chosen. Their careers were not abstract: they were built around the conviction that preventable deaths should not be accepted as inevitable.

## A young Brazilian prince with a modern career

Another passenger was **Pedro Luiz de Orléans e Bragança**, a 26-year-old descendant of Brazil’s former imperial family.

Although his ancestry drew international attention, relatives and friends emphasized that he was also a young professional building a modern life in finance. He had studied and worked abroad while maintaining close ties to Brazil and his family.

In remembrances, the royal title was often secondary to descriptions of an approachable, thoughtful young man with broad interests and a strong sense of responsibility. His death resonated in Brazil because of his family’s historical position, but those who knew him asked that he be seen not merely as a symbol of the past. He was a son, brother, cousin and friend whose future had seemed open.

## Colleagues, parents and children

Several international companies lost employees on the flight, including executives and staff from firms with operations in Brazil and Europe. Corporate statements spoke of professional ability, but co-workers often offered more personal memories: a mentor who encouraged younger employees, a colleague who made difficult assignments bearable, a manager who remembered family birthdays or brought people together across cultures.

Entire families were affected. Some passengers were traveling with spouses, parents or children. Others had relatives waiting at Charles de Gaulle Airport or expecting calls after arrival.

The presence of children and an infant deepened the sense of loss. Families asked that they be remembered not as the youngest names on a list, but through the small details that had defined them — school, play, favorite songs, family holidays and the futures imagined for them.

The 12 crew members were mourned as individuals as well. For their families and Air France colleagues, they were experienced professionals accustomed to crossing oceans and caring for travelers. Tributes recalled years of service, friendships formed through work and the routines of family life between flights.

## Mourning across continents

Memorial services were held in Brazil, France and numerous other countries. In Rio de Janeiro, relatives gathered in grief near the place where the journey had begun. In Paris, families, officials and airline employees attended services for people whose lives had converged only briefly aboard the same aircraft.

The geographic distance complicated mourning. Relatives faced long periods of uncertainty, and the recovery and identification process continued over years. Some families were eventually able to hold funerals; others had no remains to bring home.

That difference shaped each family’s grief. There was no single experience shared by all 228 families, and there was not always agreement about public ceremonies, official responses or how the tragedy should be discussed. Yet many relatives found solidarity through associations and commemorations, supporting one another across national and linguistic boundaries.

Anniversaries became occasions not only for sorrow but also for preserving memory. Names were read aloud. Photographs were displayed. Musicians performed. Colleagues established tributes. Families returned to churches, cemeteries and memorial sites, insisting that the passage of time should not turn people into statistics.

## Lives larger than the disaster

The public record of Flight 447 is inevitably tied to one night and one route across the Atlantic. For the families, however, each person’s story began long before boarding and cannot be contained by the circumstances of death.

They wanted the doctors remembered for the patients they cared for. They wanted the musicians remembered for what they created and taught. They wanted the researchers remembered for trying to make communities safer. They wanted crew members remembered for their professionalism and companionship. They wanted children remembered for the lives they had already filled with affection.

Above all, they wanted the victims recognized as individuals.

The passenger list showed who was aboard. The memorials, obituaries and stories told by loved ones showed who they were.
